Fake airdrops and trap tokens: how to spot them and what not to click

Free tokens sound great. Scammers use that: a token appears in your wallet or a post promises a reward, and the real goal is to get your signature or your seed phrase.

How the trick works

  • A token you never bought shows up in your wallet. Its name carries a website: “claim your reward at …”.
  • The site asks you to connect your wallet and sign something. That signature can give the scammer permission to move your tokens.
  • Another version asks you to pay a small “fee” or “gas” first to receive a larger reward. The reward never arrives.
  • Fake posts copy a real project's name and logo and promise an airdrop to those who “verify” their wallet.
  • Some trap tokens are honeypots: you can buy them but cannot sell.

Before you touch it

  1. Do not interact with a token you did not ask for. Do not sell it, do not click its link and do not approve anything.
  2. Look for the announcement on the project's official website and on its verified account, which you open yourself. A link from a chat does not count.
  3. Scan the contract with a tool such as GoPlus and check the token's page on CoinGecko.
  4. Read what you are asked to sign. An “approve” or “set approval for all” request can let someone move your tokens.
  5. Use a separate wallet with a small balance for anything experimental, never your main savings wallet.

What real airdrops usually look like

  • They are announced on the project's official channels, well before they happen.
  • They never ask for your seed phrase or private key.
  • They never ask you to send funds first in order to receive more.
  • They are claimed on the official domain, which you reach by typing the address yourself.

If you already signed or connected

  • Stop interacting with the site and do not enter your seed phrase anywhere to “fix” it.
  • Revoke the approvals for that wallet using a trusted approval checker.
  • Move your remaining funds to a new wallet created on a clean device.
  • Report the scam to the platform and to your local police or cybercrime unit. Keep screenshots and transaction IDs.
  • Ignore anyone offering to “recover” your funds for a fee.

Tools mentioned in this guide

  • GoPlus Security

    Checks tokens, contracts and links for common scam and honeypot risks.

    How to start (5 steps)
    1. Open the GoPlus website and find its token security checker.
    2. Choose the blockchain network the token lives on, such as Ethereum, BNB Chain, Solana or TRON.
    3. Paste the contract address. Copy it from the project's official website or from CoinGecko, not from a chat message, then run the check.
    4. Read the warnings first: honeypot (you can buy but not sell), very high buy or sell tax, an owner who can mint new tokens or change the rules, and hidden owners.
    5. If the report shows several risks, do not buy or approve anything. If it looks clean, remember that is only one input.

    A clean scan is not a guarantee. New scams are built to pass checks, and the tool cannot see the team's plans.

    Level: Beginner
    Open GoPlus Security (opens in a new tab)

  • CoinGecko

    Prices, market caps and basic data for thousands of coins.

    How to start (5 steps)
    1. Open the CoinGecko website and type the token's name or ticker in the search box.
    2. Pick the result with the right name and symbol. Fake tokens copy names, so compare the contract address on the page with the one the project publishes on its own website.
    3. Look at market cap, 24-hour trading volume and the number of markets. Very low volume, or one tiny market, means a single trade can move the price.
    4. Use the official website and social links listed on the token page, not links sent to you in a chat.
    5. Open the price chart with the longest range to see the whole history, and check which exchanges list the token.

    CoinGecko shows data. It does not tell you whether a token is safe or will rise.

    Level: Beginner
    Open CoinGecko (opens in a new tab)
